extracted.intended_audience: high-school students and teachers involved in school journalism / high-school newspaper staffs
extracted.subtask_description: A pedagogical textbook for teaching high-school students (and serving as a manual for their paper’s staff) how to gather, write, edit, and manage news for a school newspaper, including ethics, style, make-up, and business operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of a newspaper to attract and hold readers is restricted only by considerations of public welfare; use of public attention determines a newspaper’s sense of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must not use their power for selfish or unworthy purposes; they share responsibility for serving public welfare. Anti-patterns: using influence for private gain or sensationalism that harms public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Freedom of the Press
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom to discuss whatever is not explicitly forbidden by law, including critique of restrictive statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat freedom as a vital right but within legal limits. Guidance emphasizes vigorous protection of press freedom while recognizing legal boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom from all obligations except fidelity to the public interest; avoid promotion of private interests contrary to the general welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish material that advances private interests without clear public value; attribute or substantiate news communications from private sources. Anti-pattern: undisclosed sponsored content passed as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Sincerity, Truthfulness, Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Good faith with the reader is foundational; newspapers must be truthful and thorough and not be excused for lack of accuracy within their control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure thoroughness, verify facts, and avoid inaccuracies. Headlines must be fully warranted by article contents. Scoring note: accuracy in facts, names, and dates is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: News reports should be free from opinion or bias; distinguish clearly between news reporting and expressions of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion may appear in signed advocacy pieces but not in ordinary news copy. Anti-patterns: inserting editorial bias in news items, failing to separate commentary from reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Fair Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish unofficial charges affecting reputation without giving the accused an opportunity to be heard; avoid invading private rights without public-right justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give subjects chance to respond before publishing serious accusations; correct serious mistakes promptly and fully. Anti-patterns: printing allegations without verification or comment from the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Journalism — Decency
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pandering to vicious instincts by publishing sensational details of crime or vice unless demonstrably for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gratuitous publication of lurid details; weigh public good versus mere curiosity. Anti-patterns: sensational accounts published to arouse base interest rather than inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Values (general rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: News value is the capacity of a fact or idea to interest a number of people; typical factors include timeliness, unexpectedness, importance (big names/events), local interest, loss of life/property, records, contests, sentiment, and features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate how many people a story will interest — news value varies directly with the audience affected. Avoid spending much time on stories interesting to only a few. Examples: prominence (big names), timeliness, unusual events, local significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Requisites for Successful Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of required reporter competencies: (1) sympathetic and intelligent interest in people/events; (2) knowledge of where stories are found and willingness to work hard; (3) ability to distinguish news and find it; (4) power to write rapidly, accurately, and interestingly; (5) ability to estimate relative values of stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this five-point checklist to judge readiness for reporting assignments and to prioritize effort on stories with greater public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of the Good Reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential personal characteristics: accuracy; initiative; energy; tact; ambition; carefulness (grammar, spelling, punctuation); loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors expect reporters to be accurate in names/addresses, proactive in finding exclusives, ready to work long hours, courteous and neat, eager to improve, mechanically precise, and loyal to the paper/staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to Estimate Relative Values (news judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter must intuitively and correctly judge which stories merit time and prominence versus those that are trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be a representative of your readership; the stories that interest you (as an average reader) likely interest others. Use introspection and comparison with other papers to calibrate judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily Newspaper Study Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and students must read their own paper and rival papers daily to stay informed and to learn styles and avoid wasted effort on already-used stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading rivals teaches style differences and helps identify exclusive opportunities. Editors may penalize staff who start work without reading the news of the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions to Ask in Studying Newspapers (evaluation checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of questions for judging a newspaper’s merits (e.g., Do the headlines fit the stories? Do crime/scandal dominate? Are stories fair and impersonal? Are most stories of general interest? Do editorials advance worthy enterprises?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 18+ listed questions as an audit tool when comparing conservative vs sensational papers or when forming opinions on a paper’s editorial policy and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lead — completeness and strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead must be a strong beginning, complete, and give the most important facts; leads must not be overburdened and should secure interest immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead contains the essential who/what/when/where/why/how as appropriate and that the lead type (summarizing, causal, question, etc.) fits the story. Avoid packing too many details into the lead; use specialized lead forms when suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead Forms (practical rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate lead types — the book lists a dozen useful leads (summarizing/summarizing boxed, causal clause, conditional, participial, infinitive, series of simple statements, question, verse, suspense, subordinated forms, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the lead form that best suits the story’s nature and news value; examples and illustrated arrangements are provided. Anti-pattern: using a flashy lead that misrepresents the story’s substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of Material — orders and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization of story material should follow one of four orders — time, descriptive, expository, or suspense — chosen to secure clarity, interest, speed, economy, and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose order based on purpose: time order for chronological events; descriptive for scenes; expository for explanations; suspense for dramatic effect. Proper organization aids accuracy, fairness, and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the Story — clarity, unity, coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: After the lead, the body must maintain interest, be clear, coherent, unified, avoid editorializing, and support the lead with organized material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange points so that the story reads smoothly and logically, avoid padding with trivial details, keep tone impersonal in news copy, and ensure factual accuracy throughout. Examples/anti-patterns: choppy writing, editorial intrusions, exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing — requirements and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing requires preparation and temperament: ten general requirements (including appointment, knowledge of subject, note-taking, courtesy, memory, inference), responsibility to verify trustworthiness, and giving subjects a fair chance to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry notebook/pencil, know the subject’s career, avoid negative or leading questions, gain inference and verification, and cultivate tact and self-reliance. Types of persons to interview and the value of follow-ups are discussed with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation Use and Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select quotations that are accurate, meaningful, and properly attributed; startling quotations may be used in leads only when warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify exact wording, use quotations that add value or human interest, and avoid misquoting or using quotes out of context. Guidance addresses placement (lead vs body) and selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy Reading and Proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy readers must ensure mechanical perfection in grammar, spelling, punctuation, and must use standard proofreading marks and techniques to catch errors often caused by haste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread carefully despite deadline pressure; be alert to the 'demons' of grammar (e.g., subject-verb disagreement, misplaced modifiers). Use the style-sheet rules and copy marks provided. Anti-pattern: 'railroading' stories to compositors without adequate editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet Rules — punctuation, capitalization, word usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow detailed style rules (capitalization, punctuation, titles, abbreviations, dates, word combinations) and memorized lists of right/forbidden expressions (e.g., use 'more than' not 'over' for quantities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize and apply the listed cautions and preferred usages; consult the style sheet for consistency across the paper. Examples in each chapter illustrate proper/ improper usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Writing — warrant and fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should be fully warranted by the article contents and should not exaggerate or mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft headlines that attract without distorting the story; a headline that overstates is unethical and undermines accuracy. Examples discuss showy 'scare' headings vs legitimate attention-grabbing headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel and Legal Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publishing allegations that could be libelous; do not print unofficial charges affecting reputation without opportunity for the accused to be heard and without substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check facts, seek comment from accused parties, and consult legal standards before printing serious charges. Correct any factual errors promptly. Examples include treating rumors and anonymous accusations with skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy / Invasion of Private Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper should not invade private rights or feelings unless there is sure warrant of public right as distinguished from mere curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh public interest against individual privacy; avoid gratuitous exposure. Use this test before publishing personal details not necessary to the public’s understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Page Essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials should be clearly separated from news, seek advancement of worthy enterprises, avoid platitudes and irresponsible radicalism, and follow a recognized formula/classification for editorial types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep editorializing off the news page, classify editorials (three classes are discussed), and ensure editorials argue constructively and suggest reforms rather than merely attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of Editorial Staff and Roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Define staff positions (editor, associate editor, news editor, make-up editor, exchange editor, humor, sports, club editors, etc.) with clear duties and assignment schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prescribed staff structure to distribute responsibilities; maintain copy schedules and assignment lists (examples, e.g., Schedule A/B/C) to ensure efficient production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and Page Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up must follow preliminary problems and specific rules (placement of cuts, typefaces, borders, columns), with schedules for different column-width papers (Schedule A/B/C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place cuts facing in, avoid competing typefaces, ensure borders do not clutter, and follow illustrated schedules for placing stories, photos, and departments to achieve coherent layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising — typographical and ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should have clear typographical design (type faces harmonize, appropriate use of borders and cuts) and advertising staff must adhere to cautions and contract forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and improve ads from both typographic and ethical standpoints; avoid ads that recommend dubious products (wildcat stocks, questionable medicines). Keep advertising separate from news content (no free advertising in news stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and Business Management — subscription system
rubrics_metrics.description: Before subscription campaigns, prepare serially numbered subscription cards with detachable receipt stubs, file cards by room, and hold room representatives accountable for missing/ unreturned cards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the described administrative system to prevent loss/misappropriation of funds, keep accurate subscriber records, and manage distribution logistics effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Exercises and Memorization in Pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should complete exercises, memorize lists of cautions ('Right Expression to Use' lists at chapter ends), and perform readings/reports to internalize style and ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical requirement: at least one report on collateral reading; class exercises given for each chapter to practice interviewing, leads, make-up, copy-reading, and business tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Stories and Appropriate Treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and handle different story types (news, feature, interview/speech stories, sports, society, editorial), each with different leads, organization, and stylistic expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select lead form, tone, and detail level appropriate to the story type; e.g., sports need lively accounts free of meaningless slang; feature stories should truly interest readers rather than merely fill space.
